g.text: probabilistic estimation crucial for trustworthy AI
Accurate, interpretable, and unbiased probabilistic estimation is crucial to
artificial intelligence (AI) systems in mission-critical tasks that require
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Accurate, interpretable, and unbiased probabilistic estimation is crucial to artificial intelligence (AI) systems in mission-critical tasks that require trustworthy decision making.

g.text: This is because, in many real-world applications, AI systems have to work
with partial and incomplete observations that are insufficient for deductive
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) This is because, in many real-world applications, AI systems have to work with partial and incomplete observations that are insufficient for deductive and deterministic decisions (McCarthy & Hayes, 1981).

g.text: Consider the charging station planning scenario in Fig. 1, where we want to
use large language models to decide where to build a certain number of
charging stations over a region, subject to some constraints.
g.title: N3 [Context: motivating-example] (cites=0) Consider the charging station planning scenario in Fig. 1, where we want to use large language models to decide where to build a certain number of charging stations over a region, subject to some constraints.

g.text: Since we cannot always observe all the necessary information regarding a
potential location, we can only provide probability or confidence estimates
on whether we should use the candidate location.
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) Since we cannot always observe all the necessary information regarding a potential location, we can only provide probability or confidence estimates on whether we should use the candidate location.

g.text: If the number of planned stations is significant, we need to perform an
optimization process such as ILP (Roth & Yih, 2005) that maximizes the
estimated probabilities of each individual station.
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=1) If the number of planned stations is significant, we need to perform an optimization process such as ILP (Roth & Yih, 2005) that maximizes the estimated probabilities of each individual station.

g.text: A simple ranking of the candidates would not be sufficient in this scenario,
as it may yield a suboptimal solution illustrated in Fig. 1.
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) A simple ranking of the candidates would not be sufficient in this scenario, as it may yield a suboptimal solution illustrated in Fig. 1.

g.text: LLMs inaccurate and uninterpretable for probabilities
However, current LLMs are not ideal for such probability estimation tasks
since 1) LLMs tend to be inaccurate and overconfident when estimating
numerical confidences and probabilities (Xiong et al., 2024) and 2) they
g.title: N7 [Context] (cites=2) However, current LLMs are not ideal for such probability estimation tasks since 1) LLMs tend to be inaccurate and overconfident when estimating numerical confidences and probabilities (Xiong et al., 2024) and 2) they cannot provide an out-of-the-box interpretable and controllable process on how their estimates are derived (Li et al., 2024).

g.text: LLMs tend to be inaccurate and overconfident when estimating
numerical confidences and probabilities (Xiong et al., 2024)

g.text: This prevents us from using LLMs' decision-making capabilities in
g.title: N8 [Context] (cites=0) This prevents us from using LLMs' decision-making capabilities in large-scale automatic decision-making tasks.

g.text: Consequently, there is a need to find ways to infer better probabilities
g.title: N9 [Context] (cites=0) Consequently, there is a need to find ways to infer better probabilities from these models.

g.text: In this work, we propose BIRD (Bayesian Inference from Abduction and
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) In this work, we propose BIRD (Bayesian Inference from Abduction and Deduction).
N11 [Method] (cites=0) BIRD builds on three observations.

g.text: The first observation is that although LLMs cannot
they can generate neutral and comprehensive real-world
factors relevant to these probabilistic estimates.
g.title: N11a [Method: observation-1] (cites=0) The first observation is that although LLMs cannot produce convincing numerical probabilities directly, they can generate neutral and comprehensive real-world factors relevant to these probabilistic estimates.

g.text: LLMs do coarse probabilities given factors
Moreover, we observe that they can make relatively
correct coarse probability estimations when using these
factors as contexts that provide more complete
g.title: N11b [Method: observation-2] (cites=0) Moreover, we observe that they can make relatively correct coarse probability estimations when using these factors as contexts that provide more complete information.

g.text: LLMs map conditions to factors via entailment
The last observation is that LLMs can decide how
specific contexts and conditions are related to these
g.title: N11c [Method: observation-3] (cites=0) The last observation is that LLMs can decide how specific contexts and conditions are related to these factors via entailment classifications.

g.text: Together, these observations motivate BIRD, where we
approximate a Bayesian network (Friedman et al., 1997)
using LLM-generated factors, optimize its internal
conditional probabilities by sampling LLM coarse…
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=1) Together, these observations motivate BIRD, where we approximate a Bayesian network (Friedman et al., 1997) using LLM-generated factors, optimize its internal conditional probabilities by sampling LLM coarse predictions on combinations of values of all the factors, and infer more accurate probabilities for specific downstream conditions by leveraging LLMs to map conditions to factors.

g.text: formalize problem as P(Oi|C) under scenario S
As illustrated in Fig.2, we formulate the probability estimation problem as
deciding P(Oi |C), where Oi is a potential outcome (e.g., the government
should/should not build a charging station here) and C is the downstream
g.title: N18 [Method: formalization] (cites=0) As illustrated in Fig.2, we formulate the probability estimation problem as deciding P(Oi |C), where Oi is a potential outcome (e.g., the government should/should not build a charging station here) and C is the downstream condition or context (e.g., the location is on a busy highway) under a decision-making scenario S (e.g., deciding whether to build a charging station at the location).

g.text: Given S, BIRD first generates a comprehensive set of real-world factors and
values f1 , f2 , ..., fn that may contribute to the probabilistic
g.title: N19 [Method: factor-generation] (cites=0) Given S, BIRD first generates a comprehensive set of real-world factors and values f1 , f2 , ..., fn that may contribute to the probabilistic estimations.

g.text: Then, it approximates a Bayesian network structure using the generated
g.title: N20 [Method: bayesian-network] (cites=0) Then, it approximates a Bayesian network structure using the generated factors and the outcomes {O}.

g.text: We propose a novel method for estimating the conditional probability table
(CPT) for the outcome, i.e., P(Oi |f ), f ∈ F where F is the product space
of value sets for all factors.
g.title: N21 [Method: CPT-estimation] (cites=0) We propose a novel method for estimating the conditional probability table (CPT) for the outcome, i.e., P(Oi |f ), f ∈ F where F is the product space of value sets for all factors.

g.text: Specifically, we assume a set of learnable parameters P(Oi |fj )
representing the conditional probability of each possible outcome given a
g.title: N22 [Method: learnable-params] (cites=0) Specifically, we assume a set of learnable parameters P(Oi |fj ) representing the conditional probability of each possible outcome given a single variable fj .

g.text: sample f and query LLM coarse probs
We then sample f ∈ F and acquire LLM's coarse probability estimations PLLM
g.title: N23 [Method: sampling] (cites=0) We then sample f ∈ F and acquire LLM's coarse probability estimations PLLM (Oi |f ).

g.text: Next, we approximate the conditional probability Pestimated (Oi |f ) in the
CPT using the learnable parameters P(Oi |fj ) based on a derived
approximation formula and optimize these parameters by minimizing the
g.title: N24 [Method: optimization] (cites=0) Next, we approximate the conditional probability Pestimated (Oi |f ) in the CPT using the learnable parameters P(Oi |fj ) based on a derived approximation formula and optimize these parameters by minimizing the distributional distance between Pestimated (Oi |f ) and the LLM's coarse predicted probability PLLM (Oi |f ).

g.text: abduction step: align LLM with Bayesian constraints
From a high level, this abduction step aligns language models' internal
probability estimation with Bayesian constraints and has better error
g.title: N25 [Method: abduction-step] (cites=0) From a high level, this abduction step aligns language models' internal probability estimation with Bayesian constraints and has better error tolerance.

g.text: Bayesian net generic to all conditions in S
The resulting Bayesian network is generic to all possible conditions in the
g.title: N26 [Method: generic-network] (cites=0) The resulting Bayesian network is generic to all possible conditions in the scenario S.

g.text: In the following deduction step, we use the trained Bayesian parameters to
estimate the probability of any possible conditions and observations P(Oi
g.title: N27 [Method: deduction-step] (cites=0) In the following deduction step, we use the trained Bayesian parameters to estimate the probability of any possible conditions and observations P(Oi |C).

g.text: To do this, we employ an entailment process to determine P(fi |C), as shown
by "LLM Entailment" in Fig. 2, and the outcome we are interested in, P(Oi
g.title: N28 [Method: entailment-formula] (cites=0) To do this, we employ an entailment process to determine P(fi |C), as shown by "LLM Entailment" in Fig. 2, and the outcome we are interested in, P(Oi |C) = Σ_{f ∈F} P(Oi |f )P(f |C).

g.text: As we show in §4, the inferred probabilities from BIRD are more reliable,
consistent with human judgments on 30% more instances than those directly
g.title: N13 [Result] (cites=0) As we show in §4, the inferred probabilities from BIRD are more reliable, consistent with human judgments on 30% more instances than those directly predicted by LLMs.

g.text: We further show that BIRD probability predictions are good enough to be
directly used for decision making (i.e., by computing an argmax on the
predicted probabilities of each label for inference), outperforming standard
g.title: N14 [Result] (cites=1) We further show that BIRD probability predictions are good enough to be directly used for decision making (i.e., by computing an argmax on the predicted probabilities of each label for inference), outperforming standard chain-of-thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022) on several reasoning benchmarks.

g.text: More importantly, BIRD achieves better probability
estimations by optimizing an interpretable Bayesian
g.title: N15 [Contribution] (cites=0) More importantly, BIRD achieves better probability estimations by optimizing an interpretable Bayesian network with natural-language-based variables.

g.text: First, we show that BIRD-aligned probabilities can
serve as more accurate and fine-grained supervision
g.title: N16a [Contribution: benefit-1] (cites=0) First, we show that BIRD-aligned probabilities can serve as more accurate and fine-grained supervision signals for training smaller models.

g.text: In addition, we demonstrate that BIRD's factor
generation process is neutral and unbiased to the
specific conditions, so it can be used to generate
better follow-up questions to improve decision-making…
g.title: N16b [Contribution: benefit-2] (cites=0) In addition, we demonstrate that BIRD's factor generation process is neutral and unbiased to the specific conditions, so it can be used to generate better follow-up questions to improve decision-making confidence.

g.text: Combining these findings, we show that BIRD improves
mission-critical applications such as medical chatbots,
where we need reliable decisions supported with enough…
g.title: N17 [Contribution] (cites=0) Combining these findings, we show that BIRD improves trustworthiness — a crucial ability for mission-critical applications such as medical chatbots, where we need reliable decisions supported with enough evidence for high-confidence predictions.
